meanings.note: меня = me (genitive/accusative), мне = to me (dative)
Secondary conversational sense ('other forms:  (gen/acc),  (dat),  (instr),  (prep)') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

наступить.gloss: to come (of time); to step on

meanings.en: to come, to set in (night, winter, a moment)
meanings.note: Prefix 'на-' marks surface contact, accumulation, or completing a quantity (stem 'ступить'). Used in Russian as an perfective verb focusing on a single completed action or result meaning 'to come', forming an aspectual pair with 'наступать'.
Secondary conversational sense ('to step on') (наступить на + accusative) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: Ну что, Аркаша? Наступила ночь, просыпается мафия.
examples.trans: So, Arkasha? Night has fallen, the mafia wakes up.

meanings.note: Russian preposition meaning 'in' that governs a specific oblique case on the following noun phrase.
Secondary conversational sense ('into, to') (+ accusative (where to)) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: I grew up in a communal flat.
Hello! How was it in Hungary?

meanings.note: Descriptive Russian adjective meaning 'rotten', agreeing in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies.

examples.trans: It looks like some rotten potato.

examples.text: Кому нужна гнилая и чёрная картошка?
examples.trans: Who needs rotten and black potatoes?

meanings.note: Prefix 'с-' ('together' or 'down from') marks convergence or completion (stem 'лива'). Common feminine noun meaning 'plum' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: I stepped in a rotten plum.

examples.text: Я наступил в гнилую сливу, шеф.
examples.trans: I stepped in a rotten plum, chef.

meanings.note: impersonal, + genitive: денег не хватило = there wasn't enough money
Secondary conversational sense ('that's enough!') (хватит!) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: Gum? I didn't have enough money.

examples.text: Хватит спорить из-за пустяков, давайте лучше спокойно работать!
examples.trans: Enough arguing over trifles, let us just work calmly instead!

meanings.note: Russian imperfective verb expressing ongoing, habitual, or repeated action meaning 'to whine'; conjugates for person and number in the present/future and agrees in gender in the past tense.

examples.text: Хватит ныть, повара должны уметь всё!
examples.trans: Stop whining, cooks must know how to do everything!

examples.text: Хватит ныть, у меня хорошее настроение.
examples.trans: Quit whining, I am in a good mood.

meanings.note: Russian preposition meaning 'at' that governs a specific oblique case on the following noun phrase.
Secondary conversational sense ('I have') (possession) used in spoken Russian dialogue.
Secondary conversational sense ('from (ask from someone)') (просить у кого) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: Привет! Смотри, что у меня есть.

meanings.note: Agrees in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies ('good, nice').

examples.text: Какое хорошее утро! Лидия Алексеевна, чашку кофе, пожалуйста.
examples.trans: What a lovely morning! Lidia Alekseyevna, a cup of coffee, please.

meanings.note: Prefix 'на-' marks surface contact, accumulation, or completing a quantity (stem 'строение'). Verbal action/result neuter noun formed with '-ение'/'-ание'. Common neuter noun meaning 'mood, spirits' in everyday Russian.

examples.text: Вот с таким настроением и иди к Аникееву.
examples.trans: Go to Anikeev in just that mood.
I am in a good mood today.

examples.text: С таким настроением, конечно, не будет.
examples.trans: With an attitude like that, of course there won't be.

meanings.note: Invariable Russian adverb used to modify verbs or whole clauses with the sense 'today'.

examples.text: Виктор Степанович, сегодня никак не могу.
examples.trans: Viktor Stepanovich, I really can't today.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian pronoun ('you') whose case form reflects its grammatical role in the clause.
Secondary conversational sense ('other forms:  (gen/acc),  (dat),  (instr),  (prep)') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: Dad, did you bring any gum?

meanings.note: Prefix 'у-' marks departure, removal, or successful completion (stem 'знать'). Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'to recognise; to find out', paired with 'узнавать'.
Secondary conversational sense ('to find out, to learn') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: I'll find out where he is.
You recognised me. Thanks for seeing me.

meanings.note: Declinable neuter noun meaning 'art', changing its case ending across all six Russian grammatical cases to mark its role in the clause.

examples.trans: Read The Art of War, by Sun Tzu!
She loves modern art very much.
This is a real culinary work of art!

meanings.note: Prefix 'по-' forms perfective verbs or marks a brief/onset action (stem 'купать'). Used in Russian as an imperfective verb expressing ongoing, habitual, or repeated action meaning 'to buy', forming an aspectual pair with 'купить'.

meanings.en: to bribe, to buy someone off (fig.)
meanings.note: Secondary conversational sense ('to bribe, to buy someone off (fig.)') used in spoken Russian dialogue.
Declinable feminine noun meaning 'fish', changing its case ending across all six Russian grammatical cases to mark its role in the clause.

examples.trans: A big platter of fish and crabs.

examples.trans: For dinner we cooked fresh fish.

examples.text: У нас есть большая тарелка рыбы и крабов.
examples.trans: We have a big platter of fish and crabs.

meanings.note: Manner or predicative adverb in '-о' derived from the corresponding adjective stem, used in everyday speech to mean 'how much'.
Secondary conversational sense ('what a lot of!') (in exclamations) used in spoken Russian dialogue.
на днях = in the next few days, or the other day

examples.trans: I'll call in the next few days.

meanings.note: alone: 'я этого не хочу' = I don't want that

examples.trans: I'm sick of this communal flat.

examples.trans: I'm sick of this communal flat! Our pipe has been leaking for a week now.

meanings.note: Prefix 'про-' indicates movement through, completion, or missing the mark (stem 'давец'). Common masculine noun meaning 'shop assistant, seller' in everyday Russian.
Secondary conversational sense ('seller') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: A sales assistant in a phone shop.
A sales assistant in a phone shop?

говорить.gloss: to speak, to say, to talk

meanings.note: Russian imperfective verb expressing ongoing, habitual, or repeated action meaning 'to speak', forming an aspectual pair with 'сказать'; conjugates for person and number in the present/future and agrees in gender in the past tense.
Secondary conversational sense ('to speak, to talk') used in spoken Russian dialogue.
High-frequency Russian pronoun ('what') whose case form reflects its grammatical role in the clause.
Secondary conversational sense ('that') (conjunction) used in spoken Russian dialogue.
Secondary conversational sense ('? = well?') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: Привет! Смотри, что у меня есть.

examples.trans: Dad, did you bring any gum?

meanings.note: Prefix 'с-' ('together' or 'down from') marks convergence or completion (stem 'мотреть'). Used in Russian as an imperfective verb expressing ongoing, habitual, or repeated action meaning 'to look', forming an aspectual pair with 'посмотреть'.
Secondary conversational sense ('to watch') (TV, a film) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: Привет! Смотри, что у меня есть.

meanings.note: Manner/predicative adverb in '-о', derived from the neuter short form of the corresponding adjective.

examples.text: И, Марина Сергеевна, читайте всё внимательно! Особенно мелким шрифтом!

meanings.note: Invariable Russian adverb used to modify verbs or whole clauses with the sense 'so'.
verb: Что это значит? = What does it mean?
Invariable Russian adverb used to modify verbs or whole clauses with the sense 'at least'.

examples.trans: The fish is at least three days old.

examples.text: Значит, этой рыбе минимум три дня.
examples.trans: That means this fish is at least three days old.

meanings.note: Russian numeral ('three') that declines for case and governs case agreement on the counted noun.

examples.trans: We give him three days. That's it.

meanings.note: Coordinating or subordinating Russian conjunction meaning 'and', linking clauses in spoken dialogue.
Secondary conversational sense ('so, and what about') (starting a question: а жвачку?) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: Dad, did you bring any gum?

meanings.note: 'сейчас буду' = I'll be right there
Secondary conversational sense ('in a moment') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: Конечно, помогу. Кто у вас сейчас начальник?
examples.trans: Of course I'll help. Who's your boss now?

meanings.note: Prefix 'по-' forms perfective verbs or marks a brief/onset action (stem 'чесать'). Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'to scratch'.

examples.trans: And now he scratched his nose.

meanings.note: Declinable masculine noun meaning 'nose', changing its case ending across all six Russian grammatical cases to mark its role in the clause.

examples.text: Когда не можешь сам себе нос вытереть.
examples.trans: When you can't even wipe your own nose yourself.

examples.text: От холода у него покраснел нос.
examples.trans: His nose turned red from the cold.

examples.text: У меня скоро долгожданная пенсия на носу.
examples.trans: My long-awaited pension is right around the corner.

meanings.note: уже четыре года = for four years now

examples.text: Я уже четыре года работаю мэром.
examples.trans: I've been mayor for four years now.

meanings.note: Russian numeral ('five') that declines for case and governs case agreement on the counted noun.

examples.text: Мы же только начинаем. Через месяц будет пять тысяч.
examples.trans: But we're only just starting. In a month there'll be five thousand.

meanings.note: emphasis: вот поэтому ты и... = that's exactly why you...

examples.trans: I was born and grew up here.

examples.text: Спасибо, спасибо! Как вы все знаете, я родился и вырос в Синеозерске.
examples.trans: Thank you, thank you! As you all know, I was born and grew up in Sineozersk.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian pronoun ('she') whose case form reflects its grammatical role in the clause.

examples.text: Паша, я больше не хочу о ней слышать. Понял?
examples.trans: Pasha, I don't want to hear about her again. Understood?

meanings.note: Manner/predicative adverb in '-о', derived from the neuter short form of the corresponding adjective.
Secondary conversational sense ('exactly, precisely') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: Я точно не помню его адрес.
examples.trans: I don't remember his exact address.

examples.text: Точно, полиция была! А что с машиной?
examples.trans: That's right, the police were there! And what about the car?

meanings.note: Prefix 'за-' marks beginning an action, covering, or stopping by along the way (stem 'мораживать'). Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'to freeze'.

examples.trans: And it was definitely frozen before.

meanings.note: Invariable Russian adverb used to modify verbs or whole clauses with the sense 'earlier'.

examples.text: В моей комнате раньше дядя Миша жил.
examples.trans: Uncle Misha used to live in my room.

examples.text: Подождите. В моей комнате раньше дядя Миша жил.
examples.trans: Wait. Uncle Misha used to live in my room.

meanings.note: polite to one person, or to several people
Secondary conversational sense ('other forms:  (gen/acc),  (dat),  (instr),  (prep)') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: Спасибо, спасибо! Как вы все знаете, я родился и вырос в Синеозерске.
examples.trans: Thank you, thank you! As you all know, I was born and grew up in Sineozersk.

meanings.note: Prefix 'на-' marks surface contact, accumulation, or completing a quantity (stem 'стоящий'). Agrees in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies ('real, genuine').
Secondary conversational sense ('present, current') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: Ваня, да пойми ты наконец! Это настоящий успех.
examples.trans: Vanya, understand at last! This is real success.

meanings.note: Agentive or instrument masculine noun meaning 'technician', declining across all six Russian grammatical cases.

examples.text: Они совсем не похожи на настоящих мастеров.
examples.trans: They look nothing like real technicians.

examples.text: А какие признаки должны быть у мастеров?
examples.trans: And what signs should technicians have?

meanings.note: refers back to the subject: 'он держит своё слово' = he keeps his word

examples.text: А что я за мэр такой, который держит своё слово?
examples.trans: And what kind of mayor would I be if I kept my word?

meanings.note: Declinable neuter noun meaning 'matter', changing its case ending across all six Russian grammatical cases to mark its role in the clause.
Secondary conversational sense ('matter, business') used in spoken Russian dialogue.
Secondary conversational sense ('case (in court)') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: I have a lot to do.

examples.text: Мне некогда об этом думать. Слишком много дел.
examples.trans: I have no time to think about that. There's too much to do.

учиться.gloss: to study, to be a student; to learn

meanings.en: to study, to be a student
meanings.note: Prefix 'у-' marks departure, removal, or successful completion (stem 'читься'). Used in Russian as an imperfective verb expressing ongoing, habitual, or repeated action meaning 'to study', forming an aspectual pair with 'научиться'. The reflexive suffix '-ся'/'-сь' makes the action intransitive, reciprocal, or directed at the subject.

meanings.en: to learn how to do something
meanings.note: Secondary conversational sense ('to learn how to do something') (+ infinitive) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: Но вы же с ним учились вместе!
examples.trans: But you studied together with him!

examples.text: А я всё выучила. Я хорошо учусь.
examples.trans: And I've learned everything. I do well at school.

meanings.note: Invariable Russian adverb used to modify verbs or whole clauses with the sense 'for now'.
Secondary conversational sense ('while') (as a conjunction: пока я сплю) used in spoken Russian dialogue.
Secondary conversational sense ('bye, see you') (informal goodbye) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: Ладно, ребята, всем пока, увидимся завтра утром на смене!
examples.trans: All right, guys, bye everyone, see you tomorrow morning on shift!

meanings.note: Descriptive Russian adjective meaning 'kind', agreeing in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies.
in greetings: добрый день, добрый вечер

examples.text: Добрый вечер, Вика. С Новым годом!
examples.trans: Good evening, Vika. Happy New Year!

meanings.note: спасибо за + accusative = thank you for

examples.text: Спасибо, спасибо! Как вы все знаете, я родился и вырос в Синеозерске.
examples.trans: Thank you, thank you! As you all know, I was born and grew up in Sineozersk.

meanings.note: Russian preposition meaning 'for' that governs a specific oblique case on the following noun phrase.
Secondary conversational sense ('behind') (+ instrumental) used in spoken Russian dialogue.
Adjective formed with the common Slavic suffix '-н-' from a noun/verb root. Agrees in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies ('important').

examples.text: Я тебе утром говорил: не торопись. Это очень важный вопрос.
examples.trans: I told you this morning: don't rush. It's a very important question.
